blocks.text: What a smart chip is in Google Docs

Google calls these smart chips. A chip is more than plain text. It can point at a person, a file, a date, a calendar event, or a field that someone else should fill in. That makes a document easier to act on, because the details sit next to the words that need them.

A typed name is just text. A person chip is built from a name or an email address, so the document knows which person you mean. A date chip keeps a date in one format that you can change later. A placeholder chip marks a gap for a collaborator. Each type solves one small problem.
Google Docs on Mac runs in your browser

Google Docs has no native Mac app. You open it in a browser, usually Chrome or Edge on your Mac. Google's chip help page covers the web version, which is the one you use on a Mac. It gives no separate Mac menu path, so the steps below use the menus you see in the browser.
This matters for one reason. Google Docs has its own menu bar, under the document title. It is not the menu bar at the top of your Mac screen. Look up there for Insert and you will not find it.
Insert a chip by typing @

Typing @ is the fastest way in. Put your cursor where the chip belongs and type @. A menu opens. People appear first in the list. Below them you find the smart chips, building blocks, recent files and upcoming calendar events.

Google added an @ button on 12 December 2023. It appears on a blank line and opens the same menu, so you can click it instead of typing. Either way, the chip lands at your cursor, so click the spot first.
Narrow the @ menu by typing what you need

The menu filters as you type. Type part of a name to find a person. Type @me to add yourself. For a file, type its name or a keyword from the file. For a date, type the word or the date you want, and the menu suggests the matching chip.

items: @me adds yourself as a person chip.
Part of a name finds a person.
A file name or keyword finds a file.
@next tuesday makes a relative date chip.

blocks.text: Make a date chip and change its format

Date chips keep dates tidy. Type @today, @tomorrow or @yesterday for those days. Type @date to pick a date from the options. You can also type a specific date such as @1/1/2021, or a relative date such as @next tuesday.

After the chip is in the text, click its Settings icon to change the date format. Pick the format your readers expect. A status note and a formal memo often need different styles, so check the format before you share.

Here is a quick example. Write the words Due date, then a space, then type @next tuesday. Pick the matching date from the menu. The chip stays on the line, so you can change its format later without retyping the date.
Add a placeholder chip for a fillable field

A placeholder chip marks a spot for someone else to fill in. Use one for a client name, a due date or a budget figure in a template. Open the @ menu, select Placeholder chip, then choose the type of information the collaborator should enter.

The placeholder helps people see what goes where. It does not share the file. Google's help is clear that mentioning someone in a chip does not give them access, so share the document with the person who fills it in.
Mention people, and share the document separately

A person chip names someone in the text. It does not give that person permission to open or edit the file. If the person needs to read or edit, add them with Share. Check the access level before you send the link, so the right people can open it.
Insert third-party smart chips from other apps

Some chips come from other apps. Type @, then under the Integration section click the third-party application, or type its name after the @. Fill out the form and click Create. The app decides what the form asks for.

Third-party chips work only when the developer has enabled them. The app's add-on must also be installed, by you or by your domain administrator. Install add-ons from Extensions > Add-ons > Get Add-ons. Without the add-on, the chip still shows, but its hover details will not load.
A quicker route exists for links. Paste the URL into the text, then press Tab. The URL turns into a chip if the add-on is installed. You can also click the URL and choose Chip.
Which chip types need a Workspace account

Google's chip help page lists no account-type limits. A third-party guide says Stopwatch and Timer chips need a Workspace business or education account, and that Voting chips are for Workspace business or school accounts. The guide gives the paths as Insert > Smart chips > Stopwatch and Insert > Smart chips > Voting chip.
If a chip is missing on a personal account, that may be the reason. Treat the guide as a lead, not as Google's rule. Confirm it with your admin or Google's help before you plan around it.
Common mistakes with smart chips

items: Looking for Insert in the macOS menu bar. It sits in the Docs menu bar under the title.
Searching for a chip shortcut. Google's chip help lists none.
Assuming a person chip shares the file. It does not.
Adding a third-party chip without its add-on. The chip shows, but hover details stay empty.
Pasting a link and leaving it as a link. Press Tab to turn it into a chip.

blocks.text: Most mistakes come from assuming the chip does more than it does. A chip links information to the text. It does not change who can see the document.
Keyboard shortcuts for chips on Mac

Google's keyboard shortcut help says the shortcut list opens with ⌘ / on Mac. Press it to see the full list of Docs shortcuts. Google's chip help pages list no shortcut for chips, on Mac or on other systems.
Some sites claim a Cmd + @ shortcut. The GeeksforGeeks guide lists none, so do not rely on one. Typing @ is the reliable way in.
Putting it together in a meeting note

Start with a title line, then a blank line below it. Type @ and choose the owner from People. On the same line, type @next tuesday and pick the follow-up date. Add the agenda file by typing its name in the @ menu. Each chip carries its own detail, so the note stays readable.
When the note is ready, share it with the people it names. The chips point at them, but only sharing gives them access. Confirm each person can open the note before you send it.
What the @ menu offers

The @ menu puts People first. Then it lists eight smart chip types, followed by building blocks, recent files and upcoming calendar events. 9to5Google reported on the @ button when Google rolled it out in December 2023. It said the feature was available to all Workspace customers and personal Google Account users.

Not every chip type fits every document. Date and person chips suit notes, plans and status updates. Placeholder chips suit templates. Stopwatch, Timer and Voting may depend on your account type, as covered above.
When a chip does not behave
Most problems trace back to the cursor position, a missing add-on, or sharing. The troubleshooting list covers each one. Start with the cursor, since the @ menu only opens where you can type.
Where to go next

If your document runs long, add a table of contents so readers can jump to sections. The steps are in [how to add a table of contents in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/add-a-table-of-contents-in-google-docs). If you would rather speak your text, read [how to use voice typing in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/use-voice-typing-in-google-docs).
Smart chips are small, but they keep details next to the words that need them. Use them where a reader would otherwise have to ask.

faq.question: Can I insert a smart chip in the Google Docs app on Mac?
faq.answer: Google Docs has no native Mac app. You use it in a browser, such as Chrome or Edge on your Mac. Insert the chip in the browser with the @ menu or with Insert > Smart chips.

faq.question: What is the keyboard shortcut for smart chips on Mac?
faq.answer: Google's chip help pages list no keyboard shortcut for chips. Press ⌘ / to open the Docs shortcut list, and type @ to open the chip menu.

faq.question: Does mentioning someone in a chip give them access?
faq.answer: No. Google's help says a mention does not give access. Share the document with that person separately, using Share.

faq.question: How many smart chip types does the @ menu show?
faq.answer: The @ menu lists eight smart chip types after People. They are Date, Dropdown, Stopwatch, Timer, Task, Variable, Voting and Placeholder. 9to5Google reported the @ button rollout in December 2023.

faq.question: Do I need a Workspace account to use smart chips?
faq.answer: Google's chip help page lists no account-type limits. A third-party guide says Stopwatch, Timer and Voting chips need a Workspace business or education account. Confirm that before you plan around those chips.

faq.question: How do I add a calendar event chip?
faq.answer: Go to Insert > Smart chips > Calendar event. You can also type @ and pick an upcoming calendar event from the list. Recent files appear in the same menu.

steps.name: Open the document in Chrome or Edge
steps.text: Google Docs has no native Mac app, so open the document in a browser. Chrome or Edge on your Mac works for the chip steps below. You need edit access, because a view-only file cannot take new chips.
steps.tip: A view-only link shows the document but will not add a chip.

steps.name: Click the spot where the chip goes
steps.text: Click on the line where the chip will sit. The @ button appears on a blank line, so an empty line is the easiest place to start. Put the cursor where the chip should go before you type anything.
steps.tip: Click into the body text, not the margin. The cursor should blink where the chip will appear.

steps.name: Type @ to open the chip menu
steps.text: Type the @ sign on your keyboard. The menu opens with People at the top, followed by smart chips, building blocks, recent files and upcoming calendar events. You can also click the @ button if it shows on the blank line.
steps.tip: The @ menu appears only where you can type, so click into the text first.

steps.name: Type to narrow the list
steps.text: Keep typing to filter the menu. Type part of a name for a person, or @me for yourself. For a file, type its name or a keyword. For a date, type @today, @tomorrow, @next tuesday or a full date such as @1/1/2021.
steps.tip: Start with short search text, then add letters if the list is too long.

steps.name: Or use Insert > Smart chips
steps.text: If you prefer the menu, use the Docs menu bar under the document title. Choose Insert > Smart chips, then pick the chip type you want. For a calendar event, go to Insert > Smart chips > Calendar event.
steps.tip: The Docs menu bar sits inside the page, not in the macOS menu bar at the top of the screen.

steps.name: Set the date format or make a placeholder
steps.text: For a date chip, click the Settings icon on the chip to change the format. For a fillable field, choose Placeholder chip from the @ menu, then pick the type of information the collaborator should enter.
steps.tip: Pick the type that matches what the person should enter, so they know what to type.

steps.name: Check the chip and share the document
steps.text: Look at the chip in the text and check it reads the way you meant. A person chip does not share the document, so use Share to add anyone who needs to open or edit the file.
steps.tip: Confirm each named person has access before you send the link.

shortcuts.action: Open the list of Google Docs keyboard shortcuts on Mac
Open the smart chip menu in the document body

troubleshooting.fix: Click inside the body text on an empty line, then type @ again. Make sure the cursor is not in the title, a comment, or the Find box. If it still does not open, reload the page and try again.
The @ button appears only on a blank line, so move the cursor to an empty line. Typing @ works without the button.

troubleshooting.problem: A pasted link stays a link.
troubleshooting.fix: Press Tab right after pasting. The URL becomes a chip if the app's add-on is installed. If nothing changes, install the add-on through Extensions > Add-ons > Get Add-ons, then paste the link again.

troubleshooting.problem: A third-party chip shows, but its details do not load.
troubleshooting.fix: The app's add-on is probably missing. Install it through Extensions > Add-ons > Get Add-ons, or click Install on the chip. On a Workspace account, your domain administrator may need to install it.

troubleshooting.problem: Someone you named cannot open the document.
troubleshooting.fix: A person chip does not grant access. Click Share, add the person, and check the access level. Then send the link.

troubleshooting.problem: Stopwatch, Timer or Voting is missing from the menu.
troubleshooting.fix: A third-party guide says these chips need a Workspace business or education account. Google's chip help does not list that limit, so ask your admin or check Google's help before you plan around it.
